title: Arx
tagline: Arx is a programmable transaction firewall and policy engine for on-chain AI agents.
description:
An AI agent that can move money needs authority. The usual way to give it
authority is a private key or an API credential, which grants everything that
credential can do, for as long as it exists.

That is a poor fit for a system whose behaviour is steered by text it did not
write. A poisoned invoice tells a payment agent the supplier's banking details
have changed. The agent believes it — it is not malfunctioning, it was convinced
— and signs. Better reasoning does not fix this, because the model is the part
that can be talked into things.

The problem is not intelligence. The problem is authority.

Arx sits between the agent and the signer and answers one question: is this exact
transaction inside the authority this agent was actually granted? It normalizes
the transaction, resolves the agent's capability, evaluates policy, inspects the
transaction bytes, scores risk from explainable signals, and produces one of four
outcomes in Ledger's own vocabulary — ALLOW, DENY, ESCALATE, or ABORT. Only an
approval cryptographically bound to those exact bytes can reach the signer, and
the Ledger device remains the final boundary.

What makes it more than an allowlist is the set of checks a naive policy layer
gets wrong:

- The agent's own numbers are claims, not facts. An intent declares amountUsd;
  Arx prices the actual transaction bytes through a Chainlink feed and refuses
  the mismatch. An agent declaring $1 while moving 1000 ETH is caught.
- The recipient is often inside the calldata. In an ERC-20 transfer the payee is
  an argument, not the `to` field, so an allowlisted token contract is otherwise
  an open payment channel.
- A standing allowance is authority. An approve moves nothing now and lets the
  spender move everything later, so the USD ceiling applies to it.
- Dependency failure is never permission. Every external adapter distinguishes
  "checked, clean" from "could not check". Unknown resolves to DENY or ESCALATE,
  never ALLOW. Silence is never approval.

Arx also solves the credential half of the problem. Using the Ledger Key Ring, a
capability broker seals upstream secrets and hands the agent a short-lived token
bound to a hash of the policy in force — never the API key. The agent cannot leak
what it does not hold, and tokens die the moment an operator narrows the policy.

Fourteen adversarial scenarios run as assertions, not printouts: prompt
injection, declared-value lies, calldata smuggling, address poisoning, a
double-sign race, replay, revocation mid-flight, and audit tampering. The suite
exits non-zero if any behaves differently from the documentation. A separate demo
drives a real AI agent that is genuinely prompt-injected, alongside an
unprotected control case that signs the attacker's transaction — because the
contrast is the argument.
how_its_made:
TypeScript on Bun, Fastify, Zod, SQLite via bun:sqlite, viem for EVM primitives.
The authorization kernel makes no network calls and runs no model on the decision
path, so there is no prompt in it to inject into. Every decision is a pure
function of the capability, the intent, the transaction bytes and an injected
clock, which is what makes decisions reproducible from the audit log.

Ledger is the core. The Device Management Kit (1.9.0), the Ethereum signer kit
(1.18.0), the first-party Speculos transport (1.2.1) and context-module (2.5.0)
are all pinned exactly, because the @ledgerhq packages publish a develop build
daily and a caret range drifts mid-event. Alongside the SDK path I implemented
the app-ethereum APDU protocol directly from its published specification and the
app's own C source, so the signing path is transparent and auditable rather than
opaque: BIP-32 path packing, 255-byte chunking, the EIP-2718 type-byte framing,
and the typed-transaction parity convention. Signatures are not accepted, they
are verified — the signer address is recovered from the exact signed digest and
compared to what the device reported.

Because Docker was unavailable on the development machine, I built an in-process
implementation of the app-ethereum protocol that drives the same codec and is
keyed from the published Speculos test mnemonic. It derives
0xDad77910DbDFdE764fC21FCD4E74D71bBACA6D8D — the address Ledger's own fixtures
expect for that seed — which cross-checks the request encoding, BIP-32 packing
and response parsing against an external value. That mode produces real secp256k1
signatures that verify by address recovery, so the full pipeline is demonstrable
on any machine with no hardware, while reporting emulated: true and refusing to
start in production.

The Ledger Key Ring CLI (wallet-cli ring) backs the capability broker. Its key
property is that after ring init, encrypt and decrypt need network but not the
device — which is what makes the "hosts with no USB port" story work: provision
once on a laptop, then unseal on a VPS with no hardware attached.

Integrations plug into named seams — PriceOracle, NameResolver,
RiskSignalProvider, SignerAdapter, HumanVerifier, ExecutionVenue — and every one
returns an Availability<T> that keeps "checked, clean" distinct from "could not
check". ENSv2 on Sepolia resolves allowlist entries during authorization and
binds the resolved address, so a name re-pointed between approval and signing
aborts rather than redirecting funds. Chainlink aggregators are read directly
rather than through a convenience API, because latestRoundData returns updatedAt
and that lets Arx enforce its own staleness bound.

The parts I would highlight as hacky or hard-won: hashing goes through an
RFC 8785-style canonicalizer rather than JSON.stringify, because otherwise a
digest depends on key insertion order and a reordered payload could be shaped to
match an approval bound to different bytes. Claiming an approval for signing is a
SQL compare-and-swap performed before any bytes reach the device, which is what
makes double-signing impossible under concurrency — verified with eight parallel
requests. The audit log is hash-chained so editing any historical decision
invalidates every hash after it, and GET /audit/verify recomputes the chain and
names the first break.

An adversarial audit of this repository found six real defects during the build —
including a $100M standing allowance passing a $500 ceiling, and one agent being
able to sign another agent's approval. All six are fixed, each with a test, and
they are listed in the README rather than quietly patched.
auto_summary: A TypeScript service that authorizes AI-agent-initiated blockchain transactions with policy checks before Ledger- or simulator-based signing.
